questions.title: Single-Thread Execution Bottleneck
questions.prompt: Why does Redis execute single-threaded command processing faster than traditional multi-threaded locked data structures?

options.text: It bypasses CPU RAM and reads directly from NVMe disks.
options.explanation: Redis is an in-memory data store operating in RAM.

options.text: It eliminates CPU lock contention, thread context switching overhead, and lock queues while using OS epoll I/O multiplexing.
options.explanation: Correct! Running commands sequentially on a single thread avoids thread locking overhead.

rubric.excellent: Identifies lock contention, CPU context switching reduction, and epoll multiplexing.
rubric.gap: Confuses disk storage with in-memory operation.

questions.sampleSolution: Redis avoids thread synchronization overhead by processing commands sequentially on one thread.
questions.explanation: Thread locks incur heavy CPU context switching costs under high QPS.

questions.title: Atomic Counter Rate Limiting Under Concurrency
questions.prompt: Why are standard Redis GET and SET operations unsafe for implementing API rate limiting across multi-threaded gateway nodes?

options.text: Redis GET and SET require disk I/O flushes that stall execution.
options.explanation: Redis is in-memory and does not flush disk on standard GET/SET.

options.text: Concurrent GET and SET calls create a race condition where multiple requests read identical counter values before incrementing, over-admitting client traffic.
options.explanation: Correct! Non-atomic read-modify-write operations allow clients to bypass rate limits.

rubric.excellent: Identifies race conditions in read-modify-write and suggests Redis Lua scripts or atomic INCR.
rubric.gap: Suggests database transactions for rate counters.

questions.sampleSolution: Non-atomic GET/SET creates race conditions across distributed nodes. Use Redis atomic INCR or Lua scripts.
questions.explanation: Atomic operations prevent concurrent worker threads from reading stale counter values.

questions.title: Message Ordering in Distributed Log Partitions
questions.prompt: How does Apache Kafka guarantee strict sequential ordering for messages delivered to consumers?

options.text: It uses a single global lock across all cluster brokers.
options.explanation: Global locks destroy distributed log throughput.

options.text: It routes messages with the same partition key to a single partition, where they are appended sequentially to a single log.
options.explanation: Correct! Sequential ordering is guaranteed per partition key.

rubric.excellent: Explains partition keys and single-partition log append ordering.
rubric.gap: Thinks global ordering across all partitions is default.

questions.sampleSolution: Kafka guarantees message order within a single partition by routing messages with identical partition keys to that partition.
questions.explanation: Per-partition sequential log appends preserve order without bottlenecking the entire cluster.

questions.title: Consistent Hashing Node Membership Changes
questions.prompt: What is the primary advantage of Consistent Hashing over standard modulo hashing (hash(K) mod N) when scaling cache cluster nodes?

options.text: It encrypts cache keys using AES-256 before hashing.
options.explanation: Consistent hashing is an allocation algorithm, not encryption.

options.text: Adding or removing a node only remaps K/N keys rather than invalidating almost all cached keys across the entire cluster.
options.explanation: Correct! Only 1/N keys are remapped on cluster membership changes.

rubric.excellent: Identifies minimal key remapping (K/N keys) and prevention of cache stampede on node scale events.

questions.sampleSolution: Consistent hashing minimizes key remapping during node additions/removals, re-allocating only K/N keys.
questions.explanation: Standard modulo hashing remaps ~100% of keys when N changes, causing massive cache invalidation.

questions.title: B+ Tree vs LSM-Tree Storage Engine Trade-Offs
questions.prompt: Why do high-throughput write-heavy storage engines (like RocksDB and Cassandra) use LSM-Trees instead of traditional B+ Trees?

options.text: B+ Trees do not support string data types.
options.explanation: B+ Trees support arbitrary data types.

options.text: LSM-Trees buffer writes in memory (MemTable) and write sequential SSTables to disk, eliminating random disk seek overhead during writes.
options.explanation: Correct! LSM-Trees transform expensive random disk writes into cheap sequential appends.

rubric.excellent: Explains MemTable memory buffering, sequential SSTable writes, and avoidance of random I/O seeks.
rubric.gap: Thinks B+ trees cannot run on SSDs.

questions.sampleSolution: LSM-Trees buffer writes in RAM (MemTable) and write sequential SSTable files to disk, eliminating random disk write seeks.
questions.explanation: Sequential disk writes execute up to 100x faster than random page writes in B+ Trees under heavy insert volume.

questions.title: Quorum Intersection Mathematical Guarantee
questions.prompt: In a distributed cluster of N=5 nodes, why does setting Read Quorum R=3 and Write Quorum W=3 guarantee strong consistency for all read queries?

options.text: Because 5 is a prime number.
options.explanation: Prime numbers are irrelevant to quorum intersection math.

options.text: Because R + W = 6 > 5 (N), ensuring at least one node in any read quorum set of 3 nodes overlaps with the latest write quorum set of 3 nodes.
options.explanation: Correct! Pigeonhole principle guarantees R + W > N sets intersect.

rubric.excellent: Cites R + W > N formula and explains set intersection guarantee.

questions.sampleSolution: R + W (3 + 3 = 6) exceeds total nodes N=5. By the pigeonhole principle, any read quorum of 3 nodes must include at least one node from the write quorum.
questions.explanation: Set intersection math ensures stale reads are impossible when R + W > N.

questions.title: Shard Key Hotspot Prevention
questions.prompt: Why is selecting a low-cardinality column like 'country_code' as a primary database shard key considered a dangerous architectural pitfall?

options.text: Low-cardinality keys require double the RAM per shard node.
options.explanation: Low cardinality affects data distribution across shards, not per-node RAM allocation.

options.text: Low-cardinality keys create severe data skew, concentrating millions of records onto a few hotspot shards while leaving others underutilized.
options.explanation: Correct! Low cardinality forces large volumes of traffic onto single hotspot shard databases.

rubric.excellent: Explains data skew and un-balanced traffic distribution caused by low-cardinality shard keys.

questions.sampleSolution: Low-cardinality keys like country_code force all data for large nations onto single hotspot shards. Use high-cardinality keys like user_id.
questions.explanation: High cardinality keys combined with uniform hash functions guarantee even row distribution across N database shards.

questions.title: Poison Pill Messages & Dead Letter Queues
questions.prompt: What role does a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) play in preventing infinite crash loops within message consumer worker pools?

options.text: It automatically retries corrupt messages at maximum frequency until the server runs out of disk space.
options.explanation: DLQs isolate failing messages rather than continuously retrying them.

options.text: It isolates unprocessable or malformed poison-pill messages after N failed retries, permitting the main queue to continue processing valid jobs.
options.explanation: Correct! DLQs prevent malformed payloads from blocking healthy message consumption.

rubric.excellent: Explains poison-pill message isolation and unblocking consumer processing.
rubric.gap: Confuses DLQ with main queue backpressure.

questions.sampleSolution: DLQs redirect malformed messages after maximum retries so consumer worker threads remain available for valid jobs.
questions.explanation: Without a DLQ, malformed payloads trigger continuous consumer crashes.

options.text: HNSW converts numerical vectors into plaintext strings.
options.explanation: HNSW builds graph structures over vector embeddings, not plaintext conversion.

options.text: Brute-force k-NN scales linearly O(N), whereas HNSW builds a multi-layer graph that navigates to nearest neighbors in logarithmic O(log N) time.

questions.explanation: Brute-force vector distance calculation across millions of vectors stalls CPU execution.

questions.title: Asymmetric JWT Verification
questions.prompt: Why are asymmetric RS256 (RSA) signed JWTs safer for microservice architectures than symmetric HS256 (HMAC) signed JWTs?

options.text: HS256 tokens can only be read on Windows servers.
options.explanation: JWT signature algorithms are cross-platform specifications.
